pages.name: The push
pages.text: Now a 1 N push swings back and forth, `F cos ωt`. Here `ω` is how fast the push swings, in rad/s. The rule becomes `m x″ + c x′ + k x = F cos ωt`. Every term is a force in newtons. The mass starts at rest, pushed at 1 rad/s. The trace starts lumpy, because the spring's own ringing mixes in. That ringing is the [[transient]]. It dies inside the envelope, with a 4 s time constant. By about 20 s an even swing is left.
pages.alt: push rate omega equals 1 radians a second. The rule: m x double prime, plus c x prime, plus k x, equals F cos omega t. Every term is a force in newtons. The trace starts lumpy while the ringing dies inside the envelope, then settles to an even swing by about 20 seconds. time constant 4 s. settled.

pages.name: How often
pages.task: Once it has settled, how often does the mass swing?
pages.why: The ringing is the transient, and it dies. What is left is driven by the push, so it keeps the push's time. Each derivative of a cosine at rate `ω` is a cosine at the same rate. So every term can swing at 1 rad/s and match the push at every instant. One settled swing takes 6.28 s, which is 2π ÷ 1.
pages.alt: push rate omega equals 1 radians a second. one settled swing takes 6.28 s. 2π divided by 6.28 s equals 1 radians a second, the push's rate. The trace from rest at 1 radian a second, over 30 seconds. 6.28 s.

pages.name: Three forces
pages.text: Once settled, the mass swings by a fixed size `X` at the push's rate. Every term keeps that rate. They add like AC phasors. The spring's pull `kX` points one way. Two derivatives of a cosine give `−ω²` times it. So the mass term `mω²X` points the opposite way. The damper's drag `cωX` is at right angles. End to end, they make the 1 N push. As the push rate changes, so do the arrows. At 1 rad/s the spring's arrow is much longer than the mass's, and the swing is 0.329 m.

pages.name: At 2 rad/s
pages.task: The push now swings at 2 rad/s. How big is the steady swing?
pages.why: At 2 rad/s, `mω²` = 1 × 4 = 4, the same as `k`. So the spring and mass arrows are both 4 N, and they cancel. That leaves the damper's drag `cωX` alone to match the 1 N push. So `X` = 1 ÷ (0.5 × 2) = 1 m.

pages.name: The hill
pages.text: The trace now sits above a graph of steady swing against push rate. Each setting runs the trace from rest. Once the wobble dies, its steady swing drops a dot on the graph. The dots trace a hill. They climb from 0.25 m for the slowest push to about 1 m near 2 rad/s. Then they fall to 0.08 m at 4 rad/s. The slowest push gives the spring's own stretch under 1 N. Near 2 rad/s the spring and mass terms cancel. That rate is the [[natural frequency]]. The peak there is [[resonance]].
pages.alt: Pushed at 2 radians a second, the mass settles to a steady swing, and that swing is a dot on the graph.

pages.name: A fast push
pages.task: The push now swings at 4 rad/s. How big is the steady swing?
pages.why: At 4 rad/s, `mω²` = 16 while `k` = 4. So the mass term is 16X against the spring's 4X, and they leave 12X. The damper adds `cω` = 2 at right angles. So `X` = 1 ÷ √(12² + 2²) = 1 ÷ 12.17, about 0.08 m. The push is too quick for the mass to follow.

pages.name: Damping
pages.text: The whole hill is drawn for the damping set, with a ghost of the 0.5 hill. As the damping grows, the hill drops and its top slides lower. At damping 2 the top of the hill is 0.29 m near 1.41 rad/s. More damping gives a smaller peak. The hill disappears near damping 2.83. From damping 3 the swing only shrinks as the push speeds up. Let go, the spring still rings at any damping below 4, critical damping. So ringing does not promise a hill.
pages.alt: At damping 2 the hill has a top. top of the hill.

pages.name: Heavy damping
pages.task: At damping 6, where is the steady swing largest?
pages.why: At damping 6, `c²` = 36 is well past `2mk` = 8. The drag `cω` grows with the push's speed faster than the gap between `k` and `mω²` closes. So the swing only shrinks as the push speeds up. It is largest at the slowest push, 1 ÷ √(3.94² + 1.5²), about 0.24 m. The hill disappears once `c²` passes `2mk`, at damping 2.83. That is before critical damping at 4, so a spring that still rings can have no hill.
pages.alt: damping c equals 6 newton seconds per metre. c squared equals 36 is past 2mk equals 8: no hill. largest at the slowest push: 0.24 m. The swing against the push rate, with the light damping's hill as a ghost. 0.24 m.

pages.name: The loop
pages.text: An AC supply on a series loop obeys the same equation. The 1 H coil is the mass. The 0.5 Ω resistor is the damper. The 0.25 F capacitor is the spring, because `1 ÷ C` is 4. The 1 V supply is the push. The charge follows the spring's hill. The graph plots the current, which swings `ω` times as much. It peaks at exactly 2 rad/s, where `ωL` = `1 ÷ ωC`. That is series resonance. There the current is 1 V ÷ 0.5 Ω = 2 A.

pages.name: At resonance
pages.task: A 10 V supply at 1000 rad/s, which is 159 Hz, feeds 100 mH, 10 µF and 40 Ω in series. What voltage does the capacitor see?
pages.why: `ωL` = 1000 × 0.1 = 100 Ω. `1 ÷ ωC` = 1 ÷ (1000 × 0.00001) = 100 Ω. They cancel, so only the 40 Ω holds the current back. The current is 10 ÷ 40 = 0.25 A. The capacitor sees 0.25 A × 100 Ω = 25 V. That is two and a half times the supply, so rate parts and meters for it.

pages.name: Check the units
pages.task: Someone offers `v = 12e^(−RCt)` as the answer to `dv/dt = −v ÷ RC` from 12 V. Which check catches the mistake?
pages.answer: The units: `RC × t` is in s², but an exponent has no units
pages.why: `RC` is a time, in seconds. So `RC × t` is in seconds squared. The number in a power must be plain, with no units. The right answer is `v = 12e^(−t ÷ RC)`, where `t ÷ RC` has no units. Both forms give 12 V at the start and fall to 0 V at the end, so those checks miss the slip. Putting it back into the rule catches it too: its slope is `−RC × v`, not `−v ÷ RC`.

pages.name: Bilge keels
pages.task: A ship rolls in waves that come near its own roll frequency. Bilge keels add roll damping. What happens to the roll there?
pages.answer: A smaller peak, though resonance can still occur
pages.why: At the roll frequency the swing is `F ÷ cω`. More damping gives a smaller peak. Bilge keels add some damping, not enough to remove the hill. So resonance can still occur, with a smaller roll. This straight-line rule fits only small rolls.
pages.alt: more damping lowers the peak. but a peak remains: resonance can still occur. A rolling ship with bilge keels, and its roll against the wave rate. smaller peak.
options: A smaller peak, though resonance can still occur
